desc:
The string stickers lists sticker designs separated by single commas; each design is a word of lowercase letters printed on a sticker, and you own unlimited copies of every design. You want to spell the word target.

From any sticker you may cut out individual letters (each printed letter can be used at most once) and arrange the cut-out letters freely in any order. Return the minimum number of stickers you need to cut up so that all letters of target are obtained, or -1 if it is impossible.

stickers = "ab,bc,ca", target = "aabbcc"     -> 3   (each sticker gives two of the six letters)
stickers = "xy,yz",     target = "xyzz"       -> 3
stickers = "ab,cd",     target = "abe"        -> -1  (no sticker contains e)
constraints: All strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Only the multiset of letters still missing matters, not the order of the stickers. The number of different missing-letter states is small because the target has at most 15 letters.
Search with memoisation: f(missing) = fewest stickers to cover the missing letters. Take any sticker, remove the letters it can supply and recurse.

Prune hard: always branch on the first missing letter, because some sticker in the answer must supply it, so only stickers containing that letter need to be tried. Also, ignore letters of stickers that are not in the target.
editorial: Represent the state as the counts of target letters that are still missing. The target has at most 15 letters, so there are at most 215 = 32,768 states (a state is a sub-multiset of the target). Let f(state) be the minimum number of stickers needed to cover it, with f(empty) = 0.

Transition: in any optimal solution, some sticker supplies the first missing letter, and the stickers can be used in any order. So branch only over stickers containing that letter, subtract as many letters as the sticker offers (using more letters never hurts), and recurse with one more sticker. Memoise on the state. The recursion returns infinity when no sticker has the first missing letter, and the final answer is -1 in that case.

Complexity: at most 2<sup>15</sup> states, each tries only the stickers holding one particular letter, and a transition costs O(number of distinct target letters), so roughly 2<sup>15</sup> · 50 · 15 operations in the worst case and much less in practice. Removing stickers that are dominated by another sticker (after restricting to target letters) is a cheap extra speed-up.
